findings.antecedent: Territoriality (competition for territory)
findings.consequent: Social status, population control, resource distribution
findings.quote: Territoriality is a link between social behavior (competition and dominance) and population control in many animals. Communities regulate their own numbers by the use of 'conventionalized' competition, usually among males, for territory and the accompanying rights to food and (sometimes) mates. The winners are dominant animals and acquire social status, but since they are a fraction of the population, only a few community members get access to space, scarce resources, and females, thus limiting the size of the next generation.

findings.antecedent: Intraspecific aggression
findings.consequent: Spatial dispersion of individuals, ensured nutrition sources, territoriality
findings.quote: He posited that intraspecific aggression is a crucial aspect of animal life and that it has important survival value for a community because it acts as a source of mutual repulsion among individuals of the same species (in opposition to the 'herd instinct'), causing members of a group to space out over their biotope. This ensures that its sources of nutrition are not exhausted. Territoriality is, in essence, the spatial expression of this intraspecific repulsion.

findings.antecedent: Territory
findings.consequent: Security, stimulation, identity
findings.quote: Territory provides three basic elements necessary to healthy life: security (strongest at the center of a territory), stimulation (strongest at the borders, where defense against outsiders is most likely to occur), and identity.

findings.antecedent: Social status in a local community
findings.consequent: Territory size
findings.quote: It is clear that man, with many vertebrates, often displays a positive correlation between social status in a local community and the size of his territory there.

findings.antecedent: Large territories
findings.consequent: High status
findings.quote: A confusing point is that large territories are not always associated with high status; members of the elite may trade a large country estate for a small city penthouse with no drop in status; clearly the desirability of the physical location of the territory is a mediating factor.

findings.antecedent: Crowding (no room for individual territories)
findings.consequent: Substitution of pecking order for territorial order
findings.quote: animals will sometimes substitute a pecking order (hierarchy) for a relatively democratic territorial order if crowded to the point that there is no room for individual territories (e.g., Davis', 1959, work with starlings).

findings.antecedent: Relative hierarchy (dominance on home ground)
findings.consequent: Social equalization, individual rights and liberties
findings.quote: Relative hierarchy is the important idea that the psychological phenomenon of dominance has geographic components: An individual dominates all others so long as he is on home ground; territory is thus a social equalizer for lower ranking organisms.

findings.antecedent: Territoriality
findings.consequent: Individual dispersion and group cohesion (balance of repulsive and attractive forces)
findings.quote: territoriality not only disperses individuals in space but also holds them together. Individuals are rarely dispersed as widely as possible, but to distances that reflect a balance between repulsive and attractive forces.

findings.antecedent: Territory
findings.consequent: Definition and organization of social role relationships
findings.quote: territoriality is instrumental in the definition and organization of various role relationships [Proshansky et al., 1970a, p. 180] in a community.

findings.antecedent: Territory
findings.consequent: Identity, personal idiosyncrasy, freedom of action, privacy, personal autonomy, self-realization, emotional release, self-evaluation, psychological protection, sense of control
findings.quote: A clear benefit provided by many, but not all, territories is privacy (the right of the individual to decide what information about himself should be communicated to others).

findings.antecedent: Control over defined areas of space (territoriality)
findings.consequent: Increased range of options, maximized freedom of choice, reduced crowding
findings.quote: Freedom of choice becomes a key concept in understanding privacy, territoriality and crowding [p. 182].

findings.antecedent: Work spaces on a warship
findings.consequent: Defense of space (jurisdiction/territory) by crew members
findings.quote: Roos (1968) described territoriality aboard a warship, where he observed crew members defending work spaces against one another.

findings.antecedent: Social structure (friendship patterns, power structures) within a group
findings.consequent: Spatial arrangement of beds in a boys' camp
findings.quote: the members of a group (cabin) arranged their beds spatially to reflect the social structure of the group.

findings.antecedent: Specific chairs in an old people's home (over time)
findings.consequent: Attachment, psychic and emotional significance (territoriality) for inmates
findings.quote: individual inmates became almost exclusively attached to specific chairs; they would keep to their personal seats despite considerable psychological costs and physical inconvenience in doing so.

findings.antecedent: Dominance hierarchy in a mental hospital ward
findings.consequent: Territorial behavior (space use, defense patterns)
findings.quote: the investigators attempted to relate these patterns to territorial behavior. Dominance was defined by a combination of factors: the number of personal contacts a patient made, whether he initiated these, and their duration. By dividing the ward space off into squares, and using time-sampled observations, observers noted the mobility of the patients.

findings.antecedent: Territoriality
findings.consequent: Aggressive behavior
findings.quote: The authors claimed that territoriality was related to aggression, citing the fact that of all the territory-owning patients, only three did not show aggressive behavior. A close look at the data shows that this claim is unfounded since an equal proportion of nonholders show no aggression.

findings.antecedent: Dominance (social contact, staff reports) in hospitalized children
findings.consequent: Territoriality
findings.quote: A relationship between dominance (defined by social contact and by staff reports) and territoriality was discovered, which weakly resembles the previous finding.

findings.antecedent: Home territory in a mental hospital ward
findings.consequent: Winning acts of dominance
findings.quote: these individuals won 85% of all attempted physical acts of dominance on home territory, and 55% of those off home ground. Off home ground, simple status in the ward-dominance hierarchy was a fair predictor of winning acts of dominance, whereas on home ground, status position did not predict outcome.

findings.antecedent: Territoriality in retarded boys
findings.consequent: Reduced psychological complexity, enhanced personal control, persistent aggressive defense
findings.quote: Territories were interpreted by the investigators as basic and necessary reducers of psychological complexity in the boys' lives and enhancers of personal control for them, hence the difficulty in changing behavior linked to them.

findings.antecedent: Prior territory (retarded boys)
findings.consequent: Reclaiming territory ('rigidity of spatial behavior')
findings.quote: All immediately reclaimed or tried to reclaim their old territories; this was interpreted as 'rigidity of spatial behavior' (it may simply have reflected fondness for the familiar).

findings.antecedent: Territory holding (institutionalized boys)
findings.consequent: Higher rank inside the building, lower general adjustment outside the building
findings.quote: territory holders generally held higher rank than nonholders. Interestingly, territorial fighting among the boys was associated with position in the pecking order, but was negatively associated with boys' standings on 'general adjustment' (a measure that included behavior outside the building). It appeared that 'territorial adaptation' was effective for raising status inside the building, but not for functioning on the outside.

findings.antecedent: Dominance in juvenile offenders
findings.consequent: Territoriality
findings.quote: Results showed a variable relationship between dominance and territory: A positive association appeared during the first of three unequal time periods and a (nonsignificant) negative association for the final period.

findings.antecedent: Territorial situation (hospital vs. home)
findings.consequent: Demeanor and behavior (defensive/agitated vs. at ease/accommodating)
findings.quote: Colman (1968) described striking changes in demeanor and behavior of a medical patient that occurred when the patient moved from a hospital setting to his own home. In the hospital he was typically defensive and agitated; at home he was at ease, in control and accommodating.

findings.antecedent: Cognitive status (retardate vs. normal)
findings.consequent: Space preference (filled vs. open), aggression levels
findings.quote: retardates prefer filled territorial spaces (spaces with physical objects in), while normals prefer open spaces; normals were also less aggressive.

findings.antecedent: Group size, time, group sex composition (beach users)
findings.consequent: Territory size, space per person, marker deployment
findings.quote: Group territories were found not to expand regularly with number of people in the group; instead, space per person tended to decrease as group size increased. ... Territory size increased with time in same-sex groups, but mixed groups tended to deploy markers as time passed.

findings.antecedent: Territorial defense (no trespassing signs, fences) on suburban homes
findings.consequent: Residence duration, anticipated future residence, defensive vigilance
findings.quote: Results showed that families living in defended homes had lived significantly longer on the property, but also anticipated a longer residence there in the future. ... An additional finding was that occupants of property with 'no trespassing' signs answered the door significantly faster than controls (interpreted as heightened defensive vigilance).

findings.antecedent: Dominance and leadership shifts in a college seminar group
findings.consequent: Spatial positions (territories) around a table
findings.quote: individuals' dominance ratings ... correlated nonlinearly with their positions around the seminar table ... the correlations also changed with leadership shifts in the group.

findings.antecedent: Goal (avoid others vs. actively defend claims) in library/cafeteria settings
findings.consequent: Preferred territory location
findings.quote: if students are asked to show where they would situate themselves to avoid others in the setting, they prefer territories in libraries that (a) face away from the main entrance, (b) are close to a wall, and (c) are toward the rear of the room. However, instructed to defend actively their claims, subjects locate their territories (a) facing the entrance and (b) more often in the middle of a table, or on an aisle.

findings.antecedent: Population pressure, marker type, neighbor interaction, claimant absence duration in a library
findings.consequent: Marker effectiveness, neighbor support for marked claims
findings.quote: At moderate density, most objects (including library journals, books) were found to protect a single space claim totally, and to delay occupation of the rest of the table. Under heavy demand for space, more personal markers (personal jackets, sweaters) were more effective than impersonal ones. ... neighbors would only support a marked claim if directly asked, and (b) the longer the original claimant was gone, the less the neighbor would support his claim against an invader.

findings.antecedent: Marked vs. unmarked tables in a college library
findings.consequent: Preference, time spent, interpretation of markers, spacing behavior by invaders
findings.quote: given a choice, people prefer to settle at unmarked tables than marked ones; (b) if they do settle at marked tables, people spend less time there than at clear tables. ... people interpret markers as representing the owner and as protectors of the owner's space. ... the effectiveness of a marker in reserving a space claim occurs not because it signifies an area is occupied, but because potential invaders space themselves from markers as they would from other people.

findings.antecedent: Spatial invasion of marked claims at cafeteria tables
findings.consequent: Fleeing behavior, interpretation of claims as interpersonal distance (not real territories)
findings.quote: most occupants of cafeteria places (31 out of 33) flee when spatially invaded; and they concluded that marked claims at cafeteria tables are merely expressions of comfortable interpersonal distance.

findings.antecedent: Group status and group size of obstructing groups in a hallway
findings.consequent: Passersby walking through the group
findings.quote: He found that fewer passersby walked through stationary high-status groups than low-status groups, and fewer through a group of four than a group of two.

findings.antecedent: Distance between conversing pair, sex composition of pair
findings.consequent: Invasion of space between them by passersby
findings.quote: the physical distance between a conversing pair of people in this kind of arrangement affects invasion of the space between them by passersby: Beyond four feet ... the boundary surrounding the stationary pair becomes ineffective, and passersby begin to walk between the conversationalists. ... this kind of intrusion is less frequent when the stationary conversing pair is female, or a male-female combination, than when it is male.

findings.antecedent: Invasion into temporary territories
findings.consequent: Emotional effects on invaders (agonistic facial expressions, negative mood ratings)
findings.quote: the moving invaders were emotionally affected by the experience, displaying subtle, agonistic facial expressions during the invasion, and giving negative mood ratings immediately afterwards.

findings.antecedent: Resident vs. visitor status in dormitory rooms
findings.consequent: Defensive control, 'at home' perception, territory evaluation, attribution of behavior
findings.quote: Residents reported being more resistant to the control of others ('defensive control') than did visitors to the same room. Visitors saw the residents as being more 'at home' than vice versa; and residents evaluated the physical territories more positively than did visitors. ... visitors attributed both subjects' behavior more to personality factors than did residents in the same rooms.

findings.antecedent: Prolonged social isolation, incompatibility of pair members (sailors)
findings.consequent: Social withdrawal ('cocooning'), territoriality (exclusive use of areas/furniture), spatial adaptation to stress
findings.quote: Social withdrawal between the members of each pair or 'cocooning' occurred as time progressed and territoriality (defined as the exclusive use of certain areas in the rooms or items of furniture). Territoriality was accelerated in pairs whose members were incompatible on certain traits (e.g., need dominance).

findings.antecedent: Social isolation (successful vs. aborter pairs of sailors)
findings.consequent: Territorial behavior patterns, group functioning
findings.quote: pairs of sailors able to complete a successful eight-day confinement period actually showed territorial behavior from the outset, and declined with time. By contrast, aborters of the mission started low, but rose in territorial behavior as their abort date approached... Here it appears territoriality acted as an adaptive device in group functioning.

findings.antecedent: Prior experience with a physical environment, anticipated future return to environment
findings.consequent: Distance from stranger, claimed floor space, agitation in stranger's presence
findings.quote: prior experience with the room reduced the distance subjects would stand from a stranger later introduced into the environment; (b) subjects claimed more floor space (in a model building task) when the stranger was present if they anticipated future return to the environment. Anticipation of return also produced higher levels of agitation (in a projective test) in the stranger's presence; in the same condition, the subjects also stood closer to the stranger.

findings.antecedent: Specific architectural features (e.g., number of floors, corridor arrangement) in apartment buildings
findings.consequent: Alienation among tenants, cohesion among occupants, defense of common territory, antisocial behavior
findings.quote: Newman (1972) pointed out specific architectural features in some apartment buildings that promote alienation among tenants ... he made recommendations for future designs that will promote both cohesion among building occupants and defense of common territory in and around buildings, reducing antisocial behavior there.
